title: Errors and Omissions in Lump Sum Contracts: GC Risk Review Guide 2026
summary: Errors and omissions are the top cause of construction disputes in North America. Learn how GCs review lump sum contracts to catch risk before bid day.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- Errors and omissions in contract documents are the leading cause of construction disputes in North America, according to Arcadis.
- The average North American construction dispute now costs **$60.1 million** (Arcadis Global Construction Disputes Report, 2024).
- In a lump sum contract, the GC absorbs most of that risk — drawings-first review and trade-specific scope discipline are the primary defenses.
- The Eight Habits framework helps estimating teams close the gaps that drive change orders, rework, and disputed buyout.
- AI-powered tools like[Risk Review](https://provision.com/risk-review) and[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) cut contract and spec review time by 80% while flagging risks at the exact clause or page.


Errors and omissions don't show up on bid day. They show up at buyout — or worse, in the field. By then, the lump sum price is locked and the GC owns the gap.


Arcadis ranked "errors and omissions in contract documents" as the top cause of construction disputes in North America in its 2024 Global Construction Disputes Report. The average dispute value for that year: **$60.1 million** . That's not a rounding error. That's a company-altering number.


This guide breaks down how errors and omissions create lump sum exposure, what a disciplined review process looks like, and where technology is changing what's possible before bid day.


## Why Lump Sum Contracts Amplify Errors and Omissions Risk


In a cost-plus or GMP structure, errors in the documents can often be treated as a change. In a lump sum, the baseline price is fixed. If the drawings miss a system, the GC typically eats it.


"Readily inferable" language makes this worse. Contracts often require GCs to include work that a competent contractor "should have known" was needed — even when it's missing from the drawings. Courts and arbitrators have interpreted this clause broadly. One Senior PM at a Canadian ICI GC put it plainly: *"Our construction management clients expect us to find the scope gaps in the design too now. They expect us to be designers and engineers."*


That's the real risk in a lump sum. You're not just pricing what's shown. You're pricing what's implied.


## What Errors and Omissions Actually Look Like in the Field


The big ones rarely announce themselves during bid review. They hide in drawing-to-spec conflicts, in scope sheets that reference the wrong revision, and in trade packages that rely on what the last sub "assumed."


Here are real examples from GCs interviewed for[The Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) :


- **$300,000** — Lead-lined glass omitted from a hospital imaging suite. The GC absorbed the cost under "readily inferable" contract language.
- **$400,000** — A missed roof cover board on a $50M project. Recovered only through a relational concession from the sub — not through the contract.
- **$200,000** — Wood flooring scope gap on a luxury condo. No one owned it at bid. The GC owned it at closeout.
- **$45,000** — Stone-depth mismatch between civil/structural and architectural drawings on a single slab. Caught late.


These aren't catastrophic project failures. They're the slow bleed that erodes margin across a portfolio — one scope gap at a time.


## The Review Process Most GCs Are Still Using — and Why It Falls Short


The standard lump sum contract review process at most mid-market GCs looks something like this:


1. Estimator reads through the spec book (or parts of it).
2. Pre-con flags the major commercial risks — liquidated damages, retainage, indemnification.
3. Scope sheets are drafted from a template used on the last similar job.
4. Subs are sent the bid documents and asked for pricing.
5. On bid day, gaps surface during leveling.


The problem isn't effort. It's throughput. A 2,000-page project manual reviewed under a two-week bid schedule — by two estimators already running three other pursuits — will miss things. Every time.


A 2018 study by PlanGrid and FMI found that poor project data and communication breakdowns drove **$31.3 billion** in annual U.S. rework costs, with those two causes accounting for 48% of all rework. The documents were the source of the problem then. In 2026, the documents are bigger, the bid windows are shorter, and the teams haven't grown.


## Eight Habits That Close the Gap


Across 200+ interviews with GCs conducted for[The Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/subcontract-language-scope) , the firms with the tightest margins did the same things consistently. They weren't doing more work. They were doing the right work earlier.


### 1. Drawings-First, Not Boilerplate-First


Start with what's actually shown. The drawings reveal what the spec assumed. Boilerplate templates reveal what a different project assumed — often on a different building type.


### 2. Specific Document References, Not Generic Incorporation


Scope sheets that say "as per plans and specs" are the single most-cited anti-pattern in lump sum disputes. Name the drawing number. Name the spec section. If you can't cite it, you can't enforce it.


### 3. Front-Load the Buyout Conversations


The worst time to discover a sub's scope assumption is during buyout. The second-worst time is during a change order dispute. Surface sub interpretations before bid day — in writing.


### 4. Templates as a Floor, Not a Ceiling


Scope templates are a starting point. A Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC described it as the "peanut-butter test": *"It's descriptive — bread, put it on a plate, use the open jar… You have to get to that level of detail or else they'll just be like, 'you didn't tell us that.'"*


### 5. The Pre-Bid Walk Is a Scoping Tool, Not a Courtesy


Use the site walk to verify what the drawings show. Site conditions regularly conflict with drawing assumptions on renovation and phased work. Document every discrepancy.


### 6. Sub-Specific Tailoring


A sophisticated mechanical sub needs different scope language than a small drywall shop. As one Estimating Manager at a Canadian ICI GC noted: *"We have less subs who just kind of a gentleman's agreement… they've become more quick to clarify that we're not including that one piece of scope."* Tailor your package to what that sub will exploit.


### 7. Clarifications, Not Just Exclusions


An exclusions list tells the owner what you're not doing. A clarifications section tells them what you assumed. Both matter. Most scope sheets have the first. Few have the second.


### 8. The Pre-Issue Scope Review Checkpoint


Before the scope goes to subs, someone who didn't draft it reads it against the drawings. Ten minutes of review here prevents ten weeks of RFIs later.


## Trade-Specific Errors and Omissions: Where the Money Hides


Some trades carry disproportionate scope-gap risk on lump sum projects. The following are the highest-frequency gaps documented in[The Scope Gap Playbook's trade-specific chapter](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) .


### Site and Earthwork


Geotech compaction requirements, the five-foot transition zone between structural and non-structural fill, and excavator unit-rate language are chronic sources of scope disputes. If the geotech report and the civil drawings don't agree, the GC is usually holding the difference.


### Concrete


Base plate grouting, slab assembly conflicts between structural and architectural drawings, and concrete pumping requirements (who supplies the pump?) are frequently unassigned in lump sum packages.


### Steel


Embeds and anchor bolts (cast-in vs. post-installed), hoisting and rigging responsibilities, and miscellaneous metals scattered across multiple spec sections are common omission sites.


### MEP


Generator field conditioning costs have generated "millions" in disputes across multiple projects at GCs interviewed for the playbook. Add fire-rated louvres, motor starters, and lighting controls to the list of MEP items that routinely fall between trade scopes.


### Envelope


The $400K roof cover board example cited above came from the envelope trade. Add masonry-to-storefront flashings, interior vs. exterior caulking, and fire-stopping in penetrations — all of which regularly appear in neither the envelope sub's scope nor the GC's self-perform package.


### Specialty


Lead-lined glass in medical imaging rooms, curtainwall mock-up requirements, and mass-timber material protection (the $10K glulam destroyed in a lay-down yard with no contractual protection clause) represent the long tail of specialty scope exposure.

## Building a Lump Sum Contract Review Checklist


A practical review checklist for lump sum contract risk covers five areas. This isn't exhaustive — your legal team should review indemnification and insurance provisions — but it's the framework that matters most during pre-construction.


Review Area Key Questions Risk if Missed


Scope Definition Is the scope defined by drawings, specs, or both? Which revision? Conflicting documents create undefined scope the GC absorbs


Readily Inferable Language What work is "implied" by contract? How broadly is "competent contractor" defined? GC responsible for unshown work that "should have been known"


Change Order Thresholds What triggers an eligible change? What notice periods are required? Missed notice = waived claim, even for owner-directed changes


Liquidated Damages What is the LD rate? Is there a cap? What constitutes excusable delay? Uncapped LDs on a project with design coordination delays


Drawing-to-Spec Conflicts Do the drawings and specs agree on materials, assemblies, and dimensions? Conflict defaults to higher-cost interpretation — paid by GC


Trade Scope Boundaries Is each trade's scope explicitly defined? Are handoffs between trades documented? Gaps at trade interfaces become GC self-perform cost


## What Good Looks Like: A VP's Standard for Pre-Construction Risk Review


The VPs of pre-construction with the cleanest project handoffs share one habit: they don't let scope sheets reach subs until the drawings have been read, not skimmed.


One Director of Pre-Construction at a mid-market Southeast GC described the organizational gap this way: *"Pre-con is working in the scope sheet world and project management is working in the scopes of work."* The translation failure between those two documents is where scope gaps become change orders.


A VP-level standard for lump sum risk review looks like this:


- Every scope sheet is tied to a specific drawing set revision — not "current issue."
- Every trade's scope is reviewed against what the drawings show, not what the template assumes.
- Risk flags from contract review are communicated to the field team before mobilization — not after the first RFI.
- Addenda are tracked and incorporated into scope packages before bid day — not reconciled after award.


If your pre-con team is running four pursuits simultaneously and doing this manually, they aren't doing all four of these things on all four jobs. That's not a criticism. That's math.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What are errors and omissions in a construction lump sum contract?


Errors and omissions refer to mistakes, conflicts, or missing information in contract documents — drawings, specs, and scope packages. In a lump sum contract, the GC typically absorbs the cost of these gaps because the price is fixed at award. Arcadis has ranked this category as the top cause of construction disputes in North America.


### Who bears the risk of errors and omissions in a lump sum contract?


In most lump sum structures, the GC bears primary risk for errors and omissions in the documents they priced. "Readily inferable" contract language extends this further — requiring GCs to include work that a competent contractor should have anticipated, even when it's not explicitly shown in the drawings.


### How does a GC protect itself from errors and omissions in a lump sum bid?


The primary defenses are pre-bid document review, drawing-to-spec conflict identification, specific document references in scope sheets, and written clarifications submitted with the bid. Catching gaps before bid day is the only reliable protection. After award, options are limited.


### What is the "readily inferable" clause and why does it matter?


Readily inferable language requires a GC to include work that is implied by the contract, even if not explicitly shown. Courts and arbitrators have interpreted this broadly. A $300,000 lead-lined glass omission in a hospital imaging suite — not shown on drawings — was absorbed by a GC under this clause in a documented case from The Scope Gap Playbook.


### What are the most common trade-specific scope gaps in lump sum contracts?


The highest-frequency gaps appear in MEP (generator field conditioning, motor starters, lighting controls), envelope (roof cover boards, masonry-to-storefront flashings, fire-stopping), concrete (base plate grouting, pumping responsibilities), and specialty trades (lead-lined glass, curtainwall mock-ups). These regularly fall between trade scopes in lump sum packages.


### How can AI help GCs review lump sum contracts for errors and omissions?


AI tools like Provision's Risk Review run structured checklists against the full contract and spec package, flagging risks at the exact clause or page. Accuracy on pre-built checklists is 99.5%, with an 80% reduction in review time. This allows pre-construction teams to cover more ground — faster — without relying on a single estimator's attention span across a 2,000-page document set.


### How much does missing a scope item in a lump sum contract typically cost?


Individual scope gaps on commercial projects range from $10,000 (material protection omissions) to $400,000 (missed roof cover board) to over $300,000 (lead-lined glass in a hospital imaging suite). Across a portfolio, these add up to margin erosion that compounds year over year — often without appearing as a single, visible line item.
